# Interactivity {#sec-interactivity}

{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

:::: {.slide-outcomes}
::: {.callout-note title="Learning outcomes & Chapter summary"}

1. **Navigate** a view by panning, zooming, and moving through time while retaining context.
2. **Select** observations to reveal details, highlight them, or filter the data used in a view.
3. **Choose** controls for a selection and **coordinate** its effects across multiple views.
4. **Distinguish** selecting observations from changing an encoding or calculation parameter.
5. **Combine and share** client-side interactive figures using the layout and offline-export techniques from the preceding chapter.

:::
::::

## Why bother?

An interactive figure lets readers ask questions that a static view cannot answer all at once.
They might examine a particular region, inspect an observation, compare selected groups,
or change which variable is displayed. Interactivity can help us explore data ourselves
and let others explore a figure without writing code.

## Navigating views


### Panning and zooming

Panning and zooming is useful
changes the viewing window or the state we are examining.
This is useful
when there is additional detail
that cannot be seen in a chart's
initial view,
but might be of interest to the reader.
While it would be possible
to present a single static zoomed in view of the chart,
it would quickly become unwieldley
to show multiple zoom levels in separate panels.

This basic type of interaction
also illustrates a key features of interactivity,
it enables the audience of the visualization 
to activiley explore the data an ask questions of their own;
including questions that the chart creator
might not have thought of including in a static chart.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

Altair extends the concepts of a grammar of graphics
to a grammar of interactivity,
where interactive elements are composed together in a predictable manner.
We could have built up the panning and zooming through
fundamental interactive building blocks,
but since it is such a common operation,
we can use the method `.interactive()` as a shortcut
that binds an interval selection to the position scales.
Scroll over the plot to zoom and drag to pan; double-click to reset.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-pan-zoom-alt
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

cars = pd.read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv')
alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower:Q', y='Miles_per_Gallon:Q'
).interactive()
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

`ggplot` does not have interactivity built-in to the library,
so we will need to use a few different libraries
to be add interactive features to it.
Plotly provides the `ggplotly` convenience function
which convert a ggplot figure to a plotly figure
and adds basic interactive features to it.
It would be sufficient to just use the `ggplotly`
function and its toolbar to access most functionality,
but here we show how to enable
zooming and panning by default without having to click in the panel.
You will also notice that there is a tooltip enabled by default,
more on that later.
Click the little house icon in the toolbar
to reset the axes.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-pan-zoom-gg
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

cars <- readr::read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv')
car_plot <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Miles_per_Gallon)) +
    geom_point()

ggplotly(car_plot) |>
    layout(dragmode = 'pan') |>
    config(scrollZoom = TRUE)
```

Note that while plotly provides many useful interactive feature to ggplot
its API does not aim to implement a grammar of interactivity,
but follows a more traditional design approach,
so the code we learn here will look slightly 
different from the ggplot code we have used so far.

:::

### Overview and detail

Another helpful interaction tool
it to use one chart as a navigation overview
for another chart that displays more detail.
The example below
shows how a time series can be examples below use the same S&P 500 time series.
Drag an x-interval in the lower overview to set the upper panel's scale domain.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

We are using the layout operators from @sec-figure-composition
to compose a view of the navigation overview
togeher with the more detailed chart.
Here we first define a selection
and add it to the chart.
You can click and drag in the chart (also called "brushing")
to create the selection rectangle (a "brush"),
but it is not yet linked to any functionality.
`encodings=['x']` means that our brush is only selecting
on the x-axis (i.e. the height of the brush is constant).

```{python}
#| label: interaction-overview-detail-alt
sp500 = pd.read_csv('data/vega-sp500.csv', parse_dates=['date'])

overview = alt.Chart(sp500, height=50).mark_area().encode(x='date:T', y='price:Q')
brush = alt.selection_interval(encodings=['x'])
overview.add_params(brush)
```
To make another chart respond 
based on the selection we make with the brush,
we set the domain of our detailed chart's scale
to the brush's endpoints.
Now brushing in the lower overview chart
will change the scale min and max
of the detailed upper chart:

```{python}
details = alt.Chart(sp500, height=120).mark_area().encode(
    x=alt.X('date:T').scale(domain=brush),
    y='price'
)
details & overview.add_params(brush)
```
Not that we can also scroll when hovering over the brush
to expand and shrink the selection.

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

Due to the lack of a grammar of interactivity,
we cannot reuse what we learned in @sec-figure-composition
to compose together the navigation overview and the detailed chart.
Instead,
plotly has a function named `rangeslider()`
that supplies an overview with draggable handles
used to create a selection (also called a "brush").
`hovermode = 'x'` means that our brush is only selecting
on the x-axis (i.e. the height of the brush is constant).

```{r}
#| label: interaction-plotly-rangeslider
#| out.height: 300px
sp500 <- readr::read_csv('data/vega-sp500.csv')

sp500_plot <- ggplot(sp500, aes(x = date, y = price)) + geom_area()
ggplotly(sp500_plot, dynamicTicks=TRUE) |>
    rangeslider() |>
    layout(hovermode = 'x')
```

:::

## Tooltips

Tooltips is an effective way to supply
additional information when a data point is hovered.
This can prevent overlaoding a visualization with text labels
while still providing these details on demand
when a reader asks for them.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

Enabling the tooltip of a mark,
includes all mapped encodings
in the text that pops up when hovering a point in the chart.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-tooltip-all-alt
alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle(tooltip=True).encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color='Origin',
)
```

Modifying the tooltip
involves passing a dataframe column to the tooltip encoding channel instead.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-tooltip-single-alt
alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color='Origin',
    tooltip='Name'
)
```

In contrast to most other encoding channels,
a tooltip can contain multiple fields,
passed as a list.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-tooltip-multiple-alt
alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color='Origin',
    tooltip=['Name', 'Origin']
)
```

[The Altair documentation](https://altair-viz.github.io/case_studies/numpy-tooltip-images.html)
also has examples
of how to show images in the tooltip.

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

By default,
the tooltip includes all mapped aesthetics
in the text that pops up when hovering a point in the chart.

```{r}
car_tooltip_plot <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Miles_per_Gallon, color = Origin)) +
    geom_point()
ggplotly(car_tooltip_plot)
```

`ggplotly()` uses the `text` aesthetic from ggplot for custom tooltip content,
so we must first map a dataframe column to `text` in ggplot

```{r}
#| label: interaction-ggplotly
ggplotly(car_tooltip_plot + aes(text = Name), tooltip = 'text')
```

Including multiple fields involves
manually pasting together columns with newlines
in ggplot.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-tooltip-multiple-gg
ggplotly(car_tooltip_plot + aes(text = paste(Name, Origin, sep = '<br>')), tooltip = 'text')
```

:::

<!-- TODO add drilldown through something like select of filter to show bar segements? -->

## Creating and responding to selections

A selection identifies observations of interest in a chart,
and can then trigger an effect such as highlighting or filtering of that data.
We already saw how to set up a chart's scale domain
to respond to a selections range,
and here we will see a few other ways to respond to selections as well.

### Highlighting observations

Highlighting observations means that all data is retained in the chart
but the visual styling of the selected observations
differ from that of the unselected ones.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

Let's start by creating an empty brush again.
Drag'n drop to see the brush selection rectangle.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-brush-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval()
alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color='Origin'
).add_params(brush)
```
To add a response to the condition,
we can define a condition via `alt.condition(test, if_true, if_false)`,
where the "test" condition would be if the brush is over a point or not.
In the example below, we let the selected cars retain their origin colors
while other cars become light gray.
Note that empty selections match all observations
by default.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-brush-highlight-alt

brush = alt.selection_interval()
alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin', alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

Plotly supports rectangular and lasso selections through its toolbar.
`highlight_key()` assigns a stable key to each car; `highlight()` specifies how
selected observations should be emphasized. The original observations remain visible.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-brush-highlight-gg
cars <- cars |> mutate(car_id = dplyr::row_number())
highlight_cars <- highlight_key(cars, ~car_id, group = 'single-car-highlight')
highlight_plot <- ggplot(highlight_cars,
                        aes(x = Horsepower, y = Miles_per_Gallon, color = Origin, text = Name)) +
    geom_point()
ggplotly(highlight_plot, tooltip = 'text') |>
    layout(dragmode = 'select') |>
    highlight(on = 'plotly_selected', off = 'plotly_doubleclick', opacityDim = 0.15)
```

:::

#### Click and hover selections

A point selection chooses discrete items or values rather than a continuous interval.
Here we select origins by interacting with bars representing their counts.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

Click a bar; Shift-click to select several origins.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-click-alt
click = alt.selection_point(fields=['Origin'])
alt.Chart(cars).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(click, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(click)
```

Changing the event to `mouseover` lets hovering drive the selection instead.
`toggle=False` keeps one hovered origin selected at a time.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-hover-alt
hover = alt.selection_point(fields=['Origin'], on='mouseover', toggle=False)
alt.Chart(cars).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(hover, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(hover)
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

In Plotly, the `on` event makes the same distinction between click and hover.
These bars use the same origin counts as the Altair examples.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-click-gg
origin_keys <- cars |> dplyr::count(Origin) |>
    highlight_key(~Origin, group = 'origin-count-selection')
origin_bars <- plot_ly(origin_keys, x = ~n, y = ~Origin, color = ~Origin,
                       type = 'bar', orientation = 'h')
origin_bars |> highlight(on = 'plotly_click', off = 'plotly_doubleclick', opacityDim = 0.2)
```

```{r}
#| label: interaction-hover-gg
hover_keys <- cars |> dplyr::count(Origin) |>
    highlight_key(~Origin, group = 'origin-count-hover')
plot_ly(hover_keys, x = ~n, y = ~Origin, color = ~Origin, type = 'bar', orientation = 'h') |>
    highlight(on = 'plotly_hover', off = 'plotly_doubleclick', opacityDim = 0.2)
```

:::

### Coordinating selected observations across views

Referencing the same selection in several views lets us compare the selected observations
across different encodings. This is **linked brushing**.
It is one use of coordination; the earlier overview/detail example instead coordinated scale domains.

#### Linked scatterplots

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

The first view shows fuel economy and the second weight, both against horsepower.
Brush either view and inspect those cars in the other.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-linked-global-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval()
linked_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin', alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
linked_points | linked_points.encode(y='Weight_in_lbs:Q')
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

Both ggplots use the same `highlight_key()` object, so their car identifiers link the marks.
Use the selection tool in either panel. This widget will also serve as an example of
a self-contained R dashboard to export later in the section.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-linked-brush-gg
linked_cars <- highlight_key(cars, ~car_id, group = 'linked-car-views')
linked_plot <- ggplot(linked_cars,
                      aes(Horsepower, Miles_per_Gallon, color = Origin, text = Name)) + geom_point()
linked_mpg <- ggplotly(linked_plot, tooltip = 'text')
linked_weight <- ggplotly(linked_plot + aes(y = Weight_in_lbs), tooltip = 'text') |>
    style(showlegend = FALSE)
car_dashboard <- subplot(linked_mpg, linked_weight, shareX = TRUE, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE) |>
    layout(dragmode = 'select') |>
    highlight(on = 'plotly_selected', off = 'plotly_doubleclick', opacityDim = 0.15)
car_dashboard
```

:::

#### Combining selections

Altair's default `resolve='global'` maintains one brush: drawing in the other panel replaces it.
With `resolve='union'`, each panel can retain its brush and observations selected in
**either** view are highlighted.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-linked-union-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(resolve='union')
linked_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin', alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
linked_points | linked_points.encode(y='Weight_in_lbs')
```

With `resolve='intersect'`, observations must satisfy all participating brushes.
These are specific Altair selection-resolution options; the R example above uses
one shared selection rather than implementing these per-view combinations.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-linked-intersection-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(resolve='intersect')
linked_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin', alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
linked_points | linked_points.encode(y='Weight_in_lbs')
```

#### Linking views with different encodings

Linking is based on data values or identifiers, not a requirement that both charts
use the same visual channels. An origin selected in a bar chart can also identify cars in a scatterplot.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: interaction-linked-bars-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval()
click = alt.selection_point(fields=['Origin'])
selected_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin', alt.value('lightgray')),
    opacity=alt.condition(click, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(brush)
bars = alt.Chart(cars, height=80).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(click, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(click)
selected_points & bars
```

A shared legend can provide the origin selection instead of the bars.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-linked-legend-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval()
legend = alt.selection_point(fields=['Origin'], bind='legend')
selected_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin', alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
bars = alt.Chart(cars, height=80).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()',
    y='Origin',
    color='Origin',
    opacity=alt.condition(legend, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
)
(selected_points & bars).add_params(legend)
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

These panels show the same cars and origin counts.
Suppress duplicate legend entries in the bars and toggle matching legend groups together.
This coordinates trace visibility; it does not turn the precomputed ggplot counts
into a statistic that responds to arbitrary point selections.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-plotly-shared-legend
count_plot <- ggplot(cars, aes(y = Origin, fill = Origin)) + geom_bar(width = 0.6)
count_widget <- ggplotly(count_plot) |> style(showlegend = FALSE)
car_legend_plot <- car_plot + aes(color = Origin)
car_legend_widget <- ggplotly(car_legend_plot, tooltip = 'text')
subplot(count_widget, car_legend_widget, widths = c(0.3, 0.7), titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE) |>
    layout(legend = list(groupclick = 'togglegroup'))
```

:::


### Filtering observations

Highlighting changes the visual emphasis
without changing the observations used in the view.
Filtering restricts which observations enter a layer or calculation.
We introduce this distinction before the controls, because the same control can drive either effect.

An interactive query can change not just which marks appear, but the values being summarized.
The summary must be calculated from the filtered observations in the browser.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

The brush filters the bar chart's input before counting, so the bars show the number
of selected cars in each origin. The legend still controls only opacity.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-filter-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval()
legend = alt.selection_point(fields=['Origin'], bind='legend')
selected_points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin:N', alt.value('lightgray')),
    opacity=alt.condition(legend, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(brush)
bars = alt.Chart(cars, height=80).transform_filter(brush).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(legend, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
)
(selected_points & bars).add_params(legend)
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

For this R example we use a horsepower filter to drive both views.
Plotly's native histogram trace counts the filtered rows in the browser.
This differs from converting a ggplot bar chart whose counts were already calculated in R.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-filter-counts-gg
count_cars <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(cars, key = ~as.character(car_id), group = 'car-filter-counts')
count_scatter <- plot_ly(count_cars, x = ~Horsepower, y = ~Miles_per_Gallon,
                         color = ~Origin, text = ~Name, type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers')
dynamic_counts <- plot_ly(count_cars, y = ~Origin, color = ~Origin, type = 'histogram',
                          showlegend = FALSE)
htmltools::tagList(
    crosstalk::filter_slider('car-count-hp-filter', 'Horsepower range', count_cars, ~Horsepower, step = 5),
    subplot(count_scatter, dynamic_counts, nrows = 2, heights = c(0.75, 0.25), titleX = TRUE)
)
```

:::

### Driving selections from legends

A legend can be used instead of another chart
as the input element that drives the selection.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

Click a legend entry, or Shift-click several, to highlight origins.
In this example,
we bind the legend to an opacity condition,
but it could also have been used to filter the data.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-legend-alt
legend = alt.selection_point(fields=['Origin'], bind='legend')

alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    color='Origin',
    opacity=alt.condition(legend, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(legend)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

Plotly legends are interactive by default.
Clicking an entry highlights that group
and make the other points invisible.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-legend-gg
car_legend_plot <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Horsepower, y = Miles_per_Gallon, color = Origin)) +
    geom_point()
ggplotly(car_legend_plot)
```

:::

### Driving selections from widgets

Widgets are another type of input mechanisms
that can drive a selection.
A dropdown, radio button, slider, legend, or plotted mark can define a selection;
and then the chart can respond with highlighting or filtering observations,
just like with non-widget selections.

#### Movie data for category and numeric controls

We use the full Vega movies snapshot here, rather than the smaller distribution-example dataset.
Both languages apply the same missing-value filters and create a unique row identifier.
The snapshot contains suspicious future release dates for some historical films;
inspecting a year control can expose this issue, but changing axis formatting cannot correct it.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movies-setup
movies = (
    pd.read_csv('data/vega-movies-interactivity.csv', parse_dates=['Release_Date'])
    .drop(columns=['US_DVD_Sales', 'Director', 'Source', 'Creative_Type'])
    .assign(Release_Year=lambda df: df['Release_Date'].dt.year,
            Title=lambda df: df['Title'].fillna('Untitled').astype(str))
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
movies['movie_id'] = movies.index + 1
movie_points = alt.Chart(movies).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating:Q', y='IMDB_Rating:Q', tooltip='Title:N'
)
movies.head()
```

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movies-info
movies.info()
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: interaction-movies-setup-gg
movies <- readr::read_csv('data/vega-movies-interactivity.csv') |>
    dplyr::select(-c(US_DVD_Sales, Director, Source, Creative_Type)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(Release_Year = lubridate::year(Release_Date),
          # Title = replace_na(Title, 'Untitled'),
           movie_id = dplyr::row_number())
head(movies)
```

:::

#### Dropdowns, radio buttons, and initial states

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

A legend selection works for genres too, but many genre colors make the view busy.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movie-legend-alt
select_genre = alt.selection_point(fields=['Major_Genre'], bind='legend')
movie_points.encode(
    color='Major_Genre:N', opacity=alt.condition(select_genre, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre)
```

A dropdown can select a genre without assigning a color to every category.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movie-dropdown-alt
genres = sorted(movies['Major_Genre'].dropna().unique())
dropdown = alt.binding_select(options=genres)
select_genre = alt.selection_point(fields=['Major_Genre'], bind=dropdown)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(select_genre, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre)
```

Give the control a readable label and specify an initial value to make the starting state explicit.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movie-dropdown-default-alt
select_genre = alt.selection_point(
    fields=['Major_Genre'],
    bind=alt.binding_select(name='Genre: ', options=genres),
    value=[{'Major_Genre': 'Comedy'}]
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(select_genre, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre)
```

Bind different fields of a selection to different controls.
Here a film must match both the chosen genre and rating.
The age ratings use their conceptual order rather than alphabetical order.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movie-radio-alt
mpaa_ratings = ['G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R', 'Not Rated']
select_genre_and_mpaa = alt.selection_point(
    fields=['Major_Genre', 'MPAA_Rating'],
    bind={
        'Major_Genre': alt.binding_select(name='Genre: ', options=genres),
        'MPAA_Rating': alt.binding_radio(name='MPAA rating: ', options=mpaa_ratings)
    },
    value=[{'Major_Genre': 'Comedy', 'MPAA_Rating': 'PG-13'}]
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(select_genre_and_mpaa, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre_and_mpaa)
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

These Crosstalk dropdowns operate on the same movies and fields.
They start with all movies and **filter** the points; the Altair examples above instead
highlight matches. Choose a genre and rating to see the difference in response.
Using a new shared-data group keeps this example independent of other widgets on the page.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-movie-controls-gg
movie_categories <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(movies, key = ~as.character(movie_id), group = 'movie-category-controls')
movie_category_plot <- ggplot(movie_categories,
                             aes(Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating, IMDB_Rating, text = Title)) + geom_point()
category_controls <- crosstalk::bscols(
    crosstalk::filter_select('movie-genre-filter', 'Genre', movie_categories, ~Major_Genre, multiple = FALSE),
    crosstalk::filter_select('movie-rating-filter', 'MPAA rating', movie_categories, ~MPAA_Rating, multiple = FALSE),
    widths = c(6, 6)
)
htmltools::tagList(category_controls, ggplotly(movie_category_plot, tooltip = 'text'))
```

:::

#### Sliders: equality, thresholds, and ranges

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

A point selection bound to a slider matches an **exact value**.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-rating-equality-alt
select_rating = alt.selection_point(
    fields=['Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating'],
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Tomatometer: ', min=0, max=100, step=1),
    value=[{'Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating': 50}]
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(select_rating, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_rating)
```

For a threshold, a scalar parameter is simpler. `alt.datum` refers to a field of
the current observation inside an expression.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-rating-threshold-alt
rating_cutoff = alt.param(
    value=50,
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Tomatometer below: ', min=0, max=100, step=1)
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(alt.datum.Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating < rating_cutoff,
                          alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(rating_cutoff)
```

Range, step, and initial value are separate choices.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-rating-slider-settings-alt
rating_cutoff = alt.param(
    value=15,
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Tomatometer below: ', min=10, max=60, step=5)
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(alt.datum.Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating < rating_cutoff,
                          alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(rating_cutoff)
```

:::

The same pattern can select movies released before a chosen year.
This highlights matches rather than removing the remaining movies.

#### Moving through time

We can use filtering to navigate through a sequence of data states.
Both examples use the same local Gapminder snapshot: country fertility, life expectancy,
and population from 1955 to 2005. A year control chooses the observations to display;
the x- and y-scales remain fixed so that frame changes are comparable.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

A scalar parameter stores the chosen year. This example lets the reader scrub through
the frames with a slider rather than playing them automatically.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-year-frames-alt
gap = pd.read_csv('data/vega-gapminder.csv')
frame_year = alt.param(
    value=int(gap['year'].min()),
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Year: ', min=int(gap['year'].min()),
                           max=int(gap['year'].max()), step=5)
)
alt.Chart(gap).transform_filter(alt.datum.year == frame_year).mark_circle(opacity=0.7).encode(
    x=alt.X('fertility:Q').scale(domain=[0, 9]).title('Children per woman'),
    y=alt.Y('life_expect:Q').scale(domain=[20, 90]).title('Life expectancy (years)'),
    size=alt.Size('pop:Q').scale(domain=[0, float(gap['pop'].max())], range=[10, 600]).title('Population'),
    tooltip=['country:N', 'year:O', 'fertility:Q', 'life_expect:Q']
).add_params(frame_year)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

Plotly interprets `frame` as the frame variable and `ids` as the identity to track
between frames. Use Play or choose a year on its slider.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-plotly-animation
gap <- readr::read_csv('data/vega-gapminder.csv')
gap_plot <- ggplot(gap, aes(x = fertility, y = life_expect)) +
    geom_point(aes(size = pop, frame = year, ids = country, text = country), alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 9)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(20, 90)) +
    scale_size_area(max_size = 12, limits = c(0, max(gap$pop))) +
    labs(x = 'Children per woman', y = 'Life expectancy (years)', size = 'Population')
ggplotly(gap_plot, tooltip = 'text')
```


`frame` and `ids` are Plotly extensions, not ordinary static ggplot aesthetics.
Playback emphasizes movement; choosing a frame lets the reader stop and inspect it.
For comparing several years at once, small multiples may be easier than relying on memory.


A range control selects both endpoints. Here it filters the same movie ratings,
illustrating another response to a numeric selection.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-movie-slider-gg
movie_ratings <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(movies, key = ~as.character(movie_id), group = 'movie-rating-range')
movie_rating_plot <- ggplot(movie_ratings,
                           aes(Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating, IMDB_Rating, text = Title)) + geom_point()
htmltools::tagList(
    crosstalk::filter_slider('movie-rating-range-filter', 'Tomatometer range',
                            movie_ratings, ~Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating, step = 1),
    ggplotly(movie_rating_plot, tooltip = 'text')
)
```

:::

#### Building a search widget

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
search_input = alt.param(
    value='',
    bind=alt.binding(
        input='search',
        placeholder="Car model",
        name='Search ',
    )
)
search_matches = alt.expr.test(alt.expr.regexp(search_input, "i"), alt.datum.Name)

alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower',
    y='Miles_per_Gallon',
    tooltip='Name',
    opacity=alt.when(search_matches).then(alt.value(.9)).otherwise(alt.value(0.05)),
).add_params(search_input)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
searchable_cars <- highlight_key(cars, ~Name)

p <- ggplot(
    searchable_cars,
    aes(Horsepower, Miles_per_Gallon, text = Name)
) +
    geom_point()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = 'text') |>
    highlight(selectize = TRUE, opacityDim = 0.05)
```

:::

::: {.deep-dive}

#### A widget or a chart?

We could design charts as more small, more informative widgets
by removing elements from the charts and styling them accordingly.

:::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

The multidimensional legend encodes genre and rating by position, and their count by size.
The year and runtime plots provide additional brushes.
A movie must satisfy all three selection predicates to be highlighted.
`&` between predicates means AND; between charts it means vertical composition.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-multidimensional-alt
movies_fewer_years = movies.query('1994 < Release_Year < 2030') 
top_genres = movies_fewer_years['Major_Genre'].value_counts().head(5).index
movies_clean = movies_fewer_years.query(
    "Major_Genre in @top_genres and MPAA_Rating in ['G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R']"
)
select_categories = alt.selection_point(
    fields=['Major_Genre', 'MPAA_Rating'], nearest=True
)
select_year = alt.selection_interval(encodings=['x'])
select_runtime = alt.selection_interval(encodings=['x'])
category_legend = alt.Chart(movies_clean, title='Genre and rating').mark_circle().encode(
    x=alt.X('MPAA_Rating:N').sort(['G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R']).title(''),
    y=alt.Y('Major_Genre:N').title('').axis(orient='right'),
    size=alt.Size('count()').legend(None), color=alt.Color('Major_Genre:N').legend(None),
    opacity=alt.condition(select_categories, alt.value(1), alt.value(0.2))
).properties(width=130, height=140).add_params(select_categories)
year_control = alt.Chart(movies_clean, title='Production year').mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('year(Release_Date):T').title('').axis(grid=False), y=alt.Y('count()').title('').axis(None)
).properties(width=130, height=35).add_params(select_year)
runtime_control = alt.Chart(movies_clean, title='Running time').mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running_Time_min:Q').title('').axis(grid=False), y=alt.Y('count()').title('').axis(None)
).properties(width=130, height=35).add_params(select_runtime)
scatter = alt.Chart(movies_clean).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating:Q', y='IMDB_Rating:Q', color=alt.Color('Major_Genre:N').legend(None),
    tooltip='Title:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(select_categories & select_year & select_runtime, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).properties(width=300, height=300)
movie_dashboard = (scatter | (year_control & runtime_control & category_legend)).configure_view(stroke=None)
movie_dashboard.properties(usermeta={'embedOptions': {'renderer': 'canvas'}})
```

Empty selections match all movies. Double-click a brush to clear it,
or Shift-click category combinations to retain several.
The controls summarize the fixed subset; they do not recompute each other's distributions.

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

This same idea is not possible to express in plotly,
but crosstalk can combine standard controls over the same fields and movies.
Here the controls **filter** the plot rather than fading nonmatching points.
All active conditions must be satisfied.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-movie-explorer-gg
movies_fewer_years <- movies |> dplyr::filter(Release_Year > 1994, Release_Year < 2030)
top_genres <- movies_fewer_years |> dplyr::count(Major_Genre, sort = TRUE) |>
    dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) |> dplyr::pull(Major_Genre)
movies_clean <- movies_fewer_years |>
    filter(Major_Genre %in% top_genres, MPAA_Rating %in% c('G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R'))
explorer_movies <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(movies_clean, key = ~as.character(movie_id), group = 'movie-explorer')
movie_controls <- htmltools::tagList(
    crosstalk::bscols(
        crosstalk::filter_select('explorer-genre', 'Genre', explorer_movies, ~Major_Genre),
        crosstalk::filter_select('explorer-rating', 'MPAA rating', explorer_movies, ~MPAA_Rating),
        widths = c(6, 6)
    ),
    crosstalk::bscols(
        crosstalk::filter_slider('explorer-year', 'Release year', explorer_movies, ~Release_Year, step = 1),
        crosstalk::filter_slider('explorer-runtime', 'Runtime (minutes)', explorer_movies, ~Running_Time_min, step = 5),
        widths = c(6, 6)
    )
)
explorer_plot <- ggplot(explorer_movies,
                        aes(Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating, IMDB_Rating, text = Title)) + geom_point()
movie_explorer <- htmltools::tagList(movie_controls, ggplotly(explorer_plot, tooltip = 'text'))
movie_explorer
```

::::
:::

## Changing encodings and parameters

Interactivity can also change the question or representation rather than select observations.
Choosing a genre asks which movies to emphasize; choosing a y-variable asks which
measurement to display. The same dropdown mechanism can implement either task.

### Choosing the displayed variable

Both examples return to the same cars and let us choose fuel economy, weight,
or acceleration time as the response to horsepower.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

A parameter stores the chosen column name, and a calculated field retrieves that
column's value for each car. The observations remain the same.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-variable-dropdown-alt
measurement = alt.param(
    value='Miles_per_Gallon',
    name='car_measurement',
    bind=alt.binding_select(name='Y variable: ', options=['Miles_per_Gallon', 'Weight_in_lbs', 'Acceleration'])
)
alt.Chart(cars).transform_calculate(measurement='datum[car_measurement]').mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower:Q', y=alt.Y('measurement:Q').title('Selected measurement'),
    color='Origin:N', tooltip=['Name:N', 'Origin:N', 'measurement:Q']
).add_params(measurement).properties(
    title=alt.TitleParams(text=alt.ExprRef(expr="'Horsepower versus ' + car_measurement"))
)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

Plotly can switch among prepared traces.
We prepare three measurements for each origin, then choose which traces are visible.
The metadata identifies the measurement of every trace, so the visibility mask covers
all nine traces rather than assuming one trace per variable.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-plotly-dropdown
metrics <- c('Miles_per_Gallon', 'Weight_in_lbs', 'Acceleration')
metric_plot <- plot_ly(cars, x = ~Horsepower, color = ~Origin, text = ~Name)
for (metric in metrics) {
    metric_plot <- add_trace(
        metric_plot, y = cars[[metric]], type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers',
        meta = metric, visible = metric == 'Miles_per_Gallon'
    )
}
metric_plot <- plotly_build(metric_plot)
trace_metrics <- vapply(metric_plot$x$data, function(trace) unique(trace$meta), character(1))
buttons <- lapply(metrics, function(metric) list(
    method = 'update', label = metric,
    args = list(list(visible = trace_metrics == metric), list(yaxis = list(title = metric)))
))
layout(metric_plot,
       updatemenus = list(list(type = 'dropdown', active = 0, buttons = buttons)),
       yaxis = list(title = 'Miles_per_Gallon'), legend = list(title = list(text = 'Origin')))
```

:::

### Changing a calculation or display parameter

We have already used this kind of interaction in earlier chapters:
changing histogram bin width, changing a candidate line's slope in @sec-trends,
and changing the confidence level or interval multiplier in @sec-uncertainty.
Those controls change a calculation or representation, not which observed cases are of interest.

Before adding a control, ask what it should change: the viewing window, the selection,
the observations entering a calculation, the encoding, or the calculation's parameters.
Then choose a gesture or widget that makes that effect understandable.
Keep reset behavior and the current state clear so readers can tell what they are looking at.

## Saving and sharing interactive visualizations

All the examples in this chapter run **client-side**, in the browser.
That means that they don't require a server that keeps running in the background
and the examples work after the Python or R session that created them has ended. 
This also means that we can share them without someone else
without the need for that person to know how to use R or Python.
We will use the composition and self-contained
HTML export techniques from @sec-figure-composition
to assemble and share them as offline explorers.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| eval: false
movie_dashboard.save('movie-explorer-offline.html', inline=True)
```

##### ggplot {.slide-skip}

Save the linked Plotly widget directly, or save and bundle the HTML container that
includes the movie filters as well as the plot.

```{r}
#| eval: false
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(car_dashboard, 'car-dashboard-offline.html', selfcontained = TRUE)
movie_page <- htmltools::tagList(
    htmltools::tags$head(htmltools::tags$title('Movie explorer')), movie_explorer
)
htmltools::save_html(movie_page, 'movie-explorer.html', libdir = 'movie-explorer_files')
rmarkdown::pandoc_self_contained_html('movie-explorer.html', 'movie-explorer-offline-r.html')
```

:::
